content.overview: Article 32 is the Supreme Court gateway for Public Interest Litigation to enforce Part III fundamental rights. Liberalised standing opens who may approach, but it does not enlarge Article 32 into a general public-law jurisdiction beyond fundamental rights. Private disputes dressed as PIL still fail.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Is a Part III fundamental right engaged? (2) Is the petitioner acting bona fide in public interest? (3) Why is the Supreme Court the appropriate forum rather than Article 226? (4) Is the claim a private dispute in disguise? (5) What precise writ or direction is sought?
content.study:
Core rule: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. PIL uses that gateway with liberalised standing so that disadvantaged classes and systemic Part III violations can reach the Court. The subject-matter limit remains fundamental rights.

What Article 32 supplies: Jurisdiction in the Supreme Court, the power to issue directions or orders or writs for enforcement of Part III rights, and a constitutional right to constitutional remedies. PIL does not rewrite those limits.

What liberal standing adds: A bona fide petitioner may be heard even if not personally the sole aggrieved individual, where the claim is to enforce fundamental rights of persons who cannot approach the Court or to address a public fundamental-rights wrong.

What it does not add: Article 32 is not a residual public-law court for every legal wrong. Non-Part-III grievances, ordinary civil disputes, and region-specific public duties often belong under Article 226 in the High Courts.

Forum choice: Prefer Article 32 when the core complaint is enforcement of fundamental rights at a national or Supreme Court level. Prefer Article 226 where the wrong is territorial, involves other legal rights, or High Court process is the suitable first forum.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in the text of Article 32 and Part III. Cross-read the constitutional Article 32 topic for the writ power itself. Case-law verification remains a separate gate; no holding is treated as verified solely from study text.

sections.heading: Article 32 as the Supreme Court PIL gateway
sections.body: Article 32 is both a fundamental right and a jurisdictional clause. For PIL, it is the door through which public-interest claims to enforce Part III rights enter the Supreme Court. Standing may be liberalised; the rights enforced must still be fundamental rights.

sections.heading: Subject-matter limit: Part III fundamental rights
sections.body: Liberal standing does not convert Article 32 into a court of general public-law supervision. The petition must still seek enforcement of one or more fundamental rights. Claims that are purely statutory, contractual, or service-related without a Part III anchor are outside the proper Article 32 PIL frame.

sections.heading: Liberalised standing within Article 32
sections.body: A bona fide public-interest petitioner may move the Court for enforcement of fundamental rights of persons who cannot approach effectively, or for systemic Part III violations. Bona fides and the public character of the claim remain essential; private rivalries fail.

sections.heading: Choosing Article 32 or Article 226
sections.body: Article 32 is the Supreme Court Part III forum. Article 226 is wider in the High Courts (fundamental rights and other legal rights) and is often the practical first forum for region-specific wrongs. Forum choice turns on the right engaged, the scale of the wrong, and appropriate judicial hierarchy — not on the PIL label alone.

sections.heading: Abuse filters still apply
sections.body: Private disputes, busybodies, and vague or motivated petitions may be refused under Article 32 as under Article 226. Costs may follow for misuse. See the companion topic on limits and costs.

provisions.title: Right to constitutional remedies — Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for fundamental rights
High Court writ jurisdiction — comparison forum for PIL

examples.title: Systemic Part III violation
examples.body: A bona fide petitioner approaches the Supreme Court under Article 32 alleging widespread denial of a fundamental right to a disadvantaged class that cannot litigate individually. The issue is whether Article 32 PIL is the correct gateway because Part III rights are directly engaged.

examples.title: Non-Part-III public duty
examples.body: A petition to the Supreme Court under Article 32 complains only of breach of a statutory service rule with no fundamental-right claim. The issue is whether Article 32 is the wrong forum and whether Article 226 or the statutory forum is appropriate.

examples.title: Private dispute under Article 32 label
examples.body: A commercial rival files an Article 32 'PIL' seeking cancellation of a competitor's licence without a genuine Part III public-interest claim. The issue is abuse filtering and possible costs.

hypotheticals.question: Does liberalised PIL standing allow the Supreme Court under Article 32 to hear any public grievance?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Standing may be liberalised, but Article 32 still requires enforcement of fundamental rights. Non-Part-III grievances belong elsewhere.

hypotheticals.question: When should a petitioner prefer Article 226 over Article 32?
hypotheticals.analysis: Often when the wrong is region-specific, involves other legal rights beyond Part III, or the High Court is the suitable first forum. Article 32 remains the Supreme Court Part III gateway.

distinctions.title: PIL under Article 32 vs Article 226
distinctions.left: Article 32: Supreme Court; enforcement of fundamental rights.
distinctions.right: Article 226: High Courts; fundamental rights and other legal rights for any other purpose, subject to territorial limits.

rows.right: Fundamental rights and other legal rights.

rows.left: National or Supreme Court-level Part III enforcement.

distinctions.title: Article 32 jurisdiction vs liberalised standing
distinctions.left: Article 32 jurisdiction: power and subject-matter (fundamental rights).
distinctions.right: Liberalised standing: who may move the Court in a public-interest claim.

rows.left: Is this a Part III enforcement claim in the Supreme Court?
rows.right: May this bona fide petitioner be heard for others or for the public interest?

rows.left: Wrong forum or no Article 32 claim.
rows.right: Petition may fail for want of standing or bona fides.

misconceptions.trap: PIL under Article 32 can cure any public wrong, including pure statutory breaches.
misconceptions.correction: Article 32 remains limited to enforcement of fundamental rights; liberal standing does not expand subject-matter.

misconceptions.trap: Article 32 and Article 226 are interchangeable for every PIL.
misconceptions.correction: They differ in court, rights enforceable, and typical forum fitness; choose deliberately.

misconceptions.trap: Once filed as Article 32 PIL, abuse filters no longer apply.
misconceptions.correction: Private disputes, busybodies, and motivated petitions may still be refused with costs.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should an Article 32 PIL problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the Part III right claimed. II. Confirm Supreme Court forum fitness under Article 32. III. Test liberalised standing and bona fides. IV. Compare with Article 226 if forum is contested. V. Apply abuse filters. VI. State precise relief sought for enforcement of fundamental rights.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain Public Interest Litigation under Article 32 of the Constitution.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: State Article 32 as the Supreme Court Part III gateway. Explain liberalised standing within that gateway. Stress the subject-matter limit to fundamental rights. Contrast briefly with Article 226. Note abuse filters. Conclude that PIL is standing plus Article 32, not a new writ.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Discuss PIL under Article 32. How does liberalised standing interact with the fundamental-rights limit, and when is Article 226 preferable?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Article 32 as right and jurisdiction. II. PIL as standing rule within Article 32. III. Part III subject-matter limit. IV. Liberal standing criteria and bona fides. V. Comparison with Article 226. VI. Abuse filters and costs. VII. Forum-choice analysis. VIII. Conclusion: access without expanding jurisdiction beyond fundamental rights.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions in an Article 32 PIL contain on forum and standing?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the Part III right; explain why Supreme Court enforcement is appropriate; demonstrate bona fide public interest and why the affected class cannot approach; answer any Article 226 preference objection; and separate standing from the merits prayer.
